articles.title: Once the fastest US ocean liner that carried presidents and celebrities across the Atlantic, SS United States is set to become the world’s largest artificial reef
articles.summary: The SS United States, a 990-foot ocean liner that carried presidents, dignitaries and celebrities across the Atlantic, is preparing for a final voyage
articles.body: The SS United States, a 990-foot ocean liner that carried presidents, dignitaries and celebrities across the Atlantic, is preparing for a final voyage that will take it from a historic passenger ship to an underwater attraction. More than seven decades after its maiden voyage in 1952, the vessel is scheduled to be sunk off Florida’s Gulf Coast in November 2026, where it is expected to become the world’s largest artificial reef. The deployment is planned for the second week of November, subject to final arrangements and weather conditions, according to the SS United States Conservancy.The ship is currently in Mobile, Alabama, where it has undergone environmental remediation and preparations for its planned conversion. Okaloosa County, Florida, which purchased the vessel to prevent it from being scrapped, intends to place it approximately 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin–Fort Walton Beach in the Gulf of Mexico. The project aims to create marine habitat while establishing a new attraction for divers, anglers and tourists.A record-breaking transatlantic linerThe SS United States made its maiden voyage on July 3, 1952, travelling from New York to Europe. According to the Smithsonian National Museum of American History and the ship’s conservancy, it set a transatlantic speed record on that voyage, capturing the Blue Riband, the informal distinction awarded to the fastest passenger liner crossing the Atlantic. It completed the westbound crossing in three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes, surpassing the previous record held by the British liner RMS Queen Mary.American naval architect William Francis Gibbs designed the ship, which was built at Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia. Its use of aluminium in parts of its construction helped reduce weight, while its powerful propulsion system gave it exceptional speed for a passenger liner. The vessel was also designed with national defence in mind: during the Cold War, it could potentially have been converted into a troop transport in the event of a military emergency. The US government helped fund its construction, reflecting the strategic thinking behind the project.At 990 feet long and weighing more than 53,000 tons, the ship became a symbol of American engineering and post-war maritime ambition. Its passenger lists included prominent figures from politics and entertainment, and four US presidents travelled aboard during its service: Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy and Bill Clinton. Clinton’s voyage took place when he was a Rhodes Scholar travelling to Oxford, before he became president.Why the ship stopped sailingDespite its record-breaking performance, the SS United States was overtaken by changes in transatlantic travel. Commercial aviation became faster and increasingly accessible during the 1950s and 1960s, reducing demand for lengthy ocean crossings. The ship was withdrawn from service in 1969 after 17 years of operation.Its future remained uncertain for decades. The vessel was moved to Philadelphia in 1996, where it stayed docked for nearly 30 years. Various proposals sought to restore it as a passenger ship, turn it into a hotel or transform it into a tourist attraction, but none materialised. Financial difficulties and a dispute over docking fees eventually intensified concerns that the ageing liner could be sold for scrap.Okaloosa County ultimately acquired the ship for $1 million in 2024, with the stated intention of creating an artificial reef off Florida. After leaving Philadelphia in February 2025, the vessel was towed to Mobile, where it arrived the following month for preparation. The wider project has been reported to cost approximately $10.1 million, including acquisition, transportation, environmental cleanup and deployment.From ocean liner to underwater habitatBefore the ship can be submerged, it must be prepared to ensure that hazardous materials do not contaminate the marine environment. Okaloosa County says the required environmental remediation has been completed, but final approvals from the US Army Corps of Engineers and the Environmental Protection Agency remain necessary before deployment can proceed. The November timeline should therefore be treated as a plan rather than a confirmed sinking date.Artificial reefs are submerged structures that provide surfaces and shelter for marine organisms. Over time, organisms such as algae, corals and other invertebrates can colonise suitable surfaces, attracting fish and creating habitat for marine life. The SS United States is expected to become a particularly prominent site because of its size and the potential range of underwater structures it offers. The project is also intended to strengthen the region’s diving and fishing tourism industries.The ship is expected to rest near the USS Oriskany, a former US Navy aircraft carrier that was deliberately sunk off Florida in 2006 and became a major artificial-reef diving site. The SS United States is expected to surpass the Oriskany in size, giving it the distinction of becoming the world’s largest artificial reef if the planned deployment goes ahead as announced.Not every part of the liner will disappear beneath the water. The SS United States Conservancy has retained significant components, including the ship’s iconic funnels and radar mast, for a planned land-based museum and visitor centre near Destin–Fort Walton Beach. The museum is intended to preserve the vessel’s history and engineering legacy for visitors who may later explore its underwater remains.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Unmanned tanks to spearhead combat of future, Russia takes lead with India close behind
articles.summary: Russia has fielded an unmanned tank called Shturm, which means assault, which was revealed at Center-2026, one of the large exercises the Kremlin holds
articles.body: Russia has fielded an unmanned tank called Shturm, which means assault, which was revealed at Center-2026, one of the large exercises the Kremlin holds periodically alongside Vostok, Zapad and Kavkaz. The Shturm heavy assault robotic system is based on the T-72, which the Indian Army also operates in large numbers. It is meant to breach fortified defensive lines and fight in urban areas. Testing was first reported only in July 2025, and the vehicle has been in development for roughly 15 years. Russia has now brought it at least to an initial level of readiness for operational use.The system pairs remotely operated combat vehicles with a separate crewed command vehicle, built on a T-72 or T-90 chassis and described as a mothership tank. Operating either the unmanned tank or the BMPT requires three operators, who remain inside the command vehicle. The two vehicles are meant to stay within direct line of sight, at a range of roughly three to four kilometres. The main Shturm configuration carries a shortened 125 mm gun intended for urban operations, along with a bulldozer blade and additional armour to improve protection against infantry anti-tank weapons.The Indian Army is working along similar lines. It is converting T-72 tanks into remotely operated vehicles, which is to be done through IP-based interfaces, with the aim of operating them in a manned-unmanned teaming framework, in which crewed and uncrewed assets work together to multiply combat power. The Army is seeking domestic partners to digitise the Soviet-origin platform, and has opened the challenge to industry through the Innovations for Defence Excellence's (iDEX) Aditi 4.0 programme. The IP-based interface is meant to provide a secure, resilient connectivity in contested environments, which will be resistant to jamming and cyber intrusion.The unmanned T-72s are envisioned for high-risk missions, including breaching minefields, acting as decoys to draw enemy fire, spearheading assaults, reconnaissance and patrolling in contested zones. The digitised tanks will feed real-time data into command networks, while operators and commanders retain decision authority. The Army expects manned-unmanned teaming to let it generate combat mass without exposing tank crews to lethal threats, improving survivability, tempo and operational flexibility.The T-72 has been in Indian service since 1979 and has operated across varied terrain, from the plains of Punjab and the deserts of Rajasthan to high-altitude sectors and the jungles of Sri Lanka. Successive upgrades have kept it effective, and converting it into an unmanned vehicle offers a cost-effective way to extend its life. Unlike the US and China, which are investing in entirely new platforms, India is repurposing legacy armour, in line with its push for indigenous defence innovation.Other militaries are also testing the same idea, China's Type 100 Smart Tank integrates AI-driven navigation, lidar and modular armour, and is designed to work with other robotic platforms and manned vehicles. Australia's Autonomous Tactical Light Armour System Collaborative Combat Variant (ATLAS) has demonstrated autonomy ranging from remote control to autonomous navigation, with a turret that automates detection and engagement.

articles.title: Iran calls Musk’s Starlink a ‘tool of war’, vows tighter crackdown amid US-Israel conflict
articles.summary: Iranian authorities have vowed to step up efforts to block Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service and impose further restrictions on global
articles.body: Iranian authorities have vowed to step up efforts to block Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service and impose further restrictions on global internet access as the war with the United States and Israel continues.Starlink, which allows users to bypass the extensive internet filtering imposed by Tehran, is banned in Iran on national security grounds. Possessing or using the satellite internet service can lead to imprisonment and fines, while importing and distributing its terminals carry harsher penalties.Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Cyberspace Council, has described Starlink as a “tool of war” used by Tehran’s adversaries for military coordination, espionage and intelligence gathering. He said authorities had developed several systems to disable Starlink terminals but did not disclose details of the technology.Iran Uses Jammers, GPS Spoofing To Disrupt StarlinkAn internet and telecommunications expert based in Tehran, speaking to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said Iranian authorities employ several methods to interfere with Starlink connections. These include jammers operating in different configurations, spoofed GPS signals that complicate the activation of new devices, and the identification of Starlink-related internet protocols when they connect to local services.Authorities have also stepped up efforts to seize the equipment through patrols, drone searches and raids on locations suspected of selling satellite terminals.Iran has pursued the issue internationally as well. Since 2023, it has approached the International Telecommunication Union’s Radio Regulations Board, seeking action against Starlink transmissions. On October 4, Iran’s foreign ministry summoned Norway’s ambassador to protest what it described as the failure to address unauthorised Starlink operations.Tehran warns Starlink could undermine internet controlsIranian officials have warned that satellite internet could weaken the government’s ability to control online communications because it does not depend on the country’s domestic telecommunications infrastructure.Deputy Technology Minister Mohammad Hafez Hakami warned at a governance meeting in late September that widespread Starlink use could deal a major blow to Iran’s cyberspace controls. He suggested that if the trend continued, authorities might eventually have to consider cutting electricity during a future crisis to prevent access through satellite-based services.Iranian authorities have defended internet disruptions as necessary to protect national infrastructure and prevent cyberattacks. Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said on Tuesday that officials sometimes had to reduce internet speeds because of the importance of the country’s databases and online services.You use AI every day. articles.title: What is the ‘Mother of All Bombs’? The massive US weapon in focus over Iran
articles.summary: The US military has drawn up fresh strike plans that include using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear
articles.body: The US military has drawn up fresh strike plans that include using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, CNN reported on Thursday, citing multiple US officials familiar with military planning.The plans include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), widely known as the “mother of all bombs”, which could be deployed if US president Donald Trump orders a resumption of combat operations. CNN reported that potential targets include energy infrastructure and the suspected nuclear site at Pickaxe Mountain.The report comes as the Trump administration weighs its options for ending a war that has continued for more than six months, with little indication of an imminent diplomatic breakthrough. Trump has said the US will not allow Iran to acquire a nuclear weapon, but has also faced pressure to bring the conflict to an end.One source familiar with the military planning told CNN that Trump had ordered additional strike packages covering “a lot of energy infrastructure”, with the possibility of using the MOAB. A second source said plans for attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, explicitly included the bomb.The existence of these plans does not mean a strike has been authorised. A White House official told CNN that the administration does not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist, adding that Trump “keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”.The Pentagon said it plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to carry out presidential and defence secretary directives.What is the ‘mother of all bombs’?The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. It weighs 21,600 pounds, or about 9.8 tonnes, and is designed to produce an enormous blast across a wide area.Unlike a bunker-buster designed to penetrate deep underground, the MOAB detonates before hitting the ground, projecting its blast outward. According to CNN, it can destroy an area equivalent to about nine city blocks, making it suited to large-area targets rather than deeply buried facilities.The weapon was developed during the Iraq War and was conceived in part for psychological effect: its enormous explosion was intended to intimidate enemy forces and pressure them to surrender or avoid fighting. It was designed primarily for use against large concentrations of troops and equipment, as well as hardened structures above ground.Trump first authorised its use in combat during his first presidency, when the US military dropped a MOAB on an Islamic State tunnel complex in Afghanistan in 2017. Afghan officials said the strike killed 36 Islamic State fighters and destroyed tunnels, weapons and ammunition. US and Afghan officials said no civilians were killed in that attack.Questions over whether it could hit Iran’s underground sitesDespite its destructive power, the MOAB may be of limited use against Iran’s most heavily fortified nuclear facilities.CNN reported that sources familiar with the planning questioned whether the bomb could penetrate deeply enough to destroy the suspected facilities at Pickaxe Mountain, believed to be protected by layers of granite, or other nuclear sites located far underground.One source described the weapon as effective for clearing a large area but said it was “definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead”.The bomb’s large blast radius could also raise concerns about civilian casualties if it were used against energy infrastructure near populated areas or other non-military sites.Military planners have nevertheless considered the MOAB as a possible means of applying psychological pressure on Tehran. One source told CNN that the weapon could be used to alter the conflict’s current course, even if it was unlikely to force Iran to capitulate or deliver a decisive military victory.A possible escalationThe potential use of the MOAB would mark a significant escalation in the US campaign against Iran. CNN reported that military planners have prepared a range of options as the administration searches for a way to end the conflict while securing a political outcome Trump could present as a victory.Some options have reportedly been discussed as a limited show of force before US troops withdraw from the region. articles.title: Imran Khan asked to leave India: What rights do OCI cardholders have?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Actor Imran Khan has been asked to leave India by October 28 after participating in a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Actor Imran Khan has been asked to leave India by October 28 after participating in a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in Mumbai on October 10. The notice invokes Sections 7 and 29 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, raising questions about the government's powers over foreign nationals and the rights of Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholders.The actor holds US citizenship and an OCI card. He was detained during the protest, and the action followed a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya, who alleged that Khan had violated the law by participating in the demonstration."There are thousands of Imran Khans in India. They want to live here and defame the country. Action should be taken against all such people, and they should be deported," Somaiya told reporters.What do Sections 7 and 29 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act mean?Section 7 empowers the Central Government to regulate or restrict the entry, departure or continued presence of foreign nationals in India. It also allows the government to impose conditions on their stay and movement in the country.Section 29 deals with the removal of foreign nationals from India. It provides for the removal of a foreigner in circumstances covered by the Act, including violations of its provisions or orders made under it and cases involving an adverse security report.In Khan's case, the notice reportedly directs him to leave India by October 28 following his participation in the October 10 protest. The notice and the allegations against him do not, by themselves, establish that he committed an offence."Imran Khan holds foreign citizenship and is not an Indian national. Under relevant provisions of the Foreigners/Immigration Act, foreign nationals are prohibited from participating in political protests or political activities on Indian soil," a police official said.ALSO READ: CJP's Dipke questions Imran Khan's 'Leave India' notice, cites Mary Millben's support for BJPWhat is an OCI card and what rights does it give?An Overseas Citizen of India card is granted to eligible people of Indian origin who hold foreign citizenship. Despite its name, an OCI card does not confer Indian citizenship. It provides certain privileges, including a lifelong, multiple-entry visa to India, subject to applicable rules.OCI cardholders cannot vote in Indian elections or contest elections to Parliament or state legislatures. They also remain subject to Indian laws governing foreign nationals and immigration. Their OCI status does not give them an unconditional right to remain in India.Amitraj Kaushal, advocate at the Supreme Court of India, said an OCI card provides certain privileges but does not give its holder the same constitutional and political rights as an Indian citizen."An OCI card is best understood as a long-term relationship with India and not citizenship. It gives a lifelong multiple-entry visa and parity with NRIs on travel work and property. But the Citizenship Act 1955 keeps political rights like voting and contesting elections out of its reach," Kaushal said.Can OCI cardholders participate in protests in India?The advocate further added that the law does not expressly prohibit OCI cardholders from participating in peaceful gatherings. However, the constitutional right to assemble peacefully under Article 19 is available to Indian citizens, and OCI cardholders cannot claim that right on the same basis."On protests the law is quiet rather than strict. Nothing in the Act expressly bars an OCI holder from joining a peaceful gathering. However the freedom to assemble under Article 19 is a right of citizens. An OCI holder cannot invoke it the way a citizen can. Articles 14 and 21 still apply to every person," he said.Article 14 guarantees equality before the law, while Article 21 protects life and personal liberty. Both provisions apply to every person, including foreign nationals.Kaushal said the more significant legal risk for an OCI cardholder lies in the immigration consequences of an alleged violation of Indian law."The real exposure is on the immigration side. Section 7D allows cancellation of the card if the holder breaks Indian law or acts against public interest or the country's security. This can happen only after a hearing. Separately the Centre has wide powers under the Foreigners Act to ask a foreign national to leave India," he said.Section 7D of the Citizenship Act, 1955, deals with the cancellation of OCI registration on specified grounds. This is separate from the powers available to the government under immigration and foreigners laws to regulate a foreign national's stay in India.

articles.title: A 44-year-old woman jumped into the sea from a cruise ship near Greece; 20 hours later, she was found alive in a lifebuoy, telling rescuers she wanted to disembark
articles.summary: A 44-year-old woman from El Salvador was rescued after spending around 20 hours in the Ionian Sea after jumping from Royal Caribbean's Odyssey of the Seas
articles.body: A 44-year-old woman from El Salvador was rescued after spending around 20 hours in the Ionian Sea after jumping from Royal Caribbean's Odyssey of the Seas near the Greek island of Zakynthos. The woman was found conscious inside a lifebuoy in the early hours of Saturday, October 10, after a cargo ship participating in the search spotted her in the water. According to a Greek Coast Guard spokesperson cited by AFP, she told rescuers that she had jumped because she wanted to disembark. The dramatic rescue followed an extensive search involving the Hellenic Coast Guard, the cruise ship, a helicopter and nearby vessels. She was given first aid before being taken to a hospital in Greece for medical examinations.How the woman was found after 20 hours at seaThe incident occurred early on Friday, October 9, when Odyssey of the Seas was sailing southwest of Zakynthos in the Ionian Sea. Greek authorities were alerted that a passenger had entered the water, prompting the activation of an emergency response and a search operation.The Hellenic Coast Guard deployed patrol boats, while a helicopter from the Hellenic Air Force and nearby commercial vessels assisted in the search. The cruise ship also participated in efforts to locate the missing passenger.In the early hours of Saturday, the cargo ship MSC Rossella III, which was helping with the search, spotted the woman floating inside a circular lifebuoy. A light attached to the flotation device helped the crew identify her in the dark water. She was conscious when found, and a Greek Coast Guard patrol vessel subsequently recovered her.What she told rescuers about jumping from the shipThe circumstances surrounding the incident became clearer after the rescue. A Greek Coast Guard spokesperson told AFP that the woman said she had jumped from the vessel because she wanted to disembark.The reported explanation added an unusual dimension to the incident, as the passenger was found far from the cruise ship after spending approximately 20 hours in the water. Authorities have not publicly provided a detailed account of what led her to make that decision.The woman was identified as a 44-year-old Salvadoran national. Her name was not released in the reports reviewed.How the rescue operation unfoldedThe search involved several maritime and aerial resources. After the initial alert, Coast Guard vessels and a helicopter were sent to the area, while ships nearby were asked to assist. The cruise ship also took part in the search.The discovery by MSC Rossella III proved crucial. Once the cargo ship's crew spotted the woman, they alerted the authorities and helped facilitate her recovery. Video released by the Hellenic Coast Guard showed rescuers throwing a rope towards her as she floated inside the orange lifebuoy. She grabbed the rope and pulled herself towards the rescue vessel.After being brought aboard, she received first aid. The Coast Guard then transported her to the port of Katakolo on the western coast of Greece.The woman was taken to hospital after the rescueFollowing her arrival at Katakolo, the woman was transferred by ambulance to a hospital in the nearby city of Pyrgos for medical observation and examinations.According to reporting by CBS News and AFP, a local prosecutor ordered a psychiatric evaluation as part of the subsequent assessment. The Katakolo Port Authority began investigating the circumstances of the incident.The Coast Guard confirmed that the woman was conscious when found and received first aid after being recovered. Her survival after such a prolonged period in the water drew attention to the role of the lifebuoy in keeping her afloat and making her visible to the cargo ship's crew.Royal Caribbean responds to the incidentRoyal Caribbean confirmed that a passenger had gone overboard and said it had launched a search-and-rescue effort in coordination with the authorities. The company also said its Care Team was providing support and assistance to the passenger's loved ones.The incident occurred during a Mediterranean cruise aboard Odyssey of the Seas, which had departed from Civitavecchia, Italy, on October 4 for a week-long sailing. The ship was scheduled to return to Italy on October 11.Greek authorities are investigating the circumstances of the incident, while the rescue itself remains notable for the woman's survival and the discovery that she had remained afloat inside a lifebuoy for around 20 hours.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pennsylvania owner held a Chester home for 10 years before it sold for $28,000 at a tax sale with about a $5,741 upset price; on October 13, an appeals court ordered the sale set aside over notice failures
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania man who owned a house in Chester for 10 years has won an appeal after his property was sold for $28,000 at a tax sale linked to unpaid
articles.body: A Pennsylvania man who owned a house in Chester for 10 years has won an appeal after his property was sold for $28,000 at a tax sale linked to unpaid property taxes. The Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania ruled on October 13, 2026, that the Delaware County Tax Claim Bureau had failed to make the additional efforts required by law to notify the owner before selling his property.The property, located at 113 West 23rd Street in Chester, belonged to Gang Luo. It was put up for sale on September 22, 2022, to recover unpaid City of Chester real estate taxes for 2020, as per the official court document. The upset sale price was $5,741, while the successful bidder, Gerardo Ponce, purchased the property for $28,000. An upset price includes outstanding taxes, tax liens, municipal claims and statutory costs associated with a property.Luo challenged the sale, arguing that he had not received proper notice and that the authorities had failed to locate him after an important notice was returned unclaimed. However, the Delaware County Court of Common Pleas rejected his petition in December 2023, finding that the tax bureau had followed the required procedures.Luo subsequently appealed the decision. After examining the evidence, a three-judge panel of the Commonwealth Court concluded that the bureau had not met its legal obligations. The court reversed the earlier ruling and sent the case back to the lower court with instructions to set aside the tax sale.How the Chester property was sold According to court records, Luo had owned the single-family house for approximately 10 years and rented it to a tenant. He told the trial court that he visited the property about once a month to carry out maintenance and check its condition.The tax dispute concerned unpaid real estate taxes for 2020. In his appeal, Luo referred to an unpaid city tax amount of $1,327 and questioned whether losing his property over that amount was justified.Before the September 2022 sale, the tax bureau sent notices to Luo's residential address at 498 Howellville Road in Berwyn, Pennsylvania. On August 3, it mailed a formal sale notice through certified mail with restricted delivery. However, the notice was returned marked "unclaimed".The bureau also published sale notices in newspapers and posted a notice at the Chester property on August 26. A final notice was mailed by First-Class Mail on August 29 and was not returned as undeliverable.At the October 2023 hearing, the bureau's Upset Sales Coordinator, Janine Heinlein, explained that officials believed they had Luo's correct mailing address because he had previously contacted the office about another property he owned.What the owner saidDuring the hearing, Luo explained why he had not been staying at his usual residential address for much of 2022.He testified that he had been hospitalised for a leg injury between March and May 2022. After leaving hospital, he moved into a senior-living house with his elderly parents to care for them.Although Luo confirmed that the Berwyn address was his personal residence, he denied receiving formal notice of the unpaid taxes or the impending sale of the Chester property.He also told the court that his tenant had never informed him about a notice being posted at the house. According to his testimony, he first discovered that the property had been sold on October 1, 2022, when he visited the tax bureau to enquire about another property.The trial court had rejected Luo's claim that he was unaware of the sale. However, the appeals court found that the evidence did not establish that he had received timely actual notice of the proceedings.Why appeals court found notice process inadequateUnder Pennsylvania's Real Estate Tax Sale Law, authorities must follow specific notification procedures before selling property to recover unpaid taxes.These include publishing notices, posting notices at the property and mailing notices to the owner. When a required mailed notice is returned without the owner's signature, officials must make reasonable additional efforts to locate and notify that person. The appeals court found that the bureau had failed to demonstrate such efforts in Luo's case.During testimony, Heinlein acknowledged that a search had identified a telephone number associated with Luo, but she did not say whether anyone had called it. She also confirmed that she had relied on the existing address rather than conducting further searches through other sources.The court explained that having a correct mailing address did not remove the bureau's responsibility to take additional steps once the certified notice was returned unclaimed.It also rejected the suggestion that a courtesy letter concerning another property could establish that Luo knew about the sale of the Chester house.The court stated that tax sale laws were intended primarily to ensure the collection of taxes, rather than deprive property owners of their rights.What the October 13 ruling means In its October 13 opinion, the Commonwealth Court concluded that the bureau had not established compliance with Section 607.1(a) of Pennsylvania's Real Estate Tax Sale Law. The judges also found insufficient evidence that Luo had received timely actual notice of the sale.As a result, the court reversed the December 6, 2023 ruling and directed the lower court to enter an order setting aside the tax sale.Luo had also raised constitutional objections, including an argument that the sale amounted to taking property without just compensation. However, the appeals court did not examine those remaining arguments because the notification failures were sufficient to decide the case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Pakistan tests Fatah-II ballistic missile, same type intercepted during Operation Sindoor
articles.summary: Pakistan's Army has test-launched the Fatah-2 Extended Range hypersonic ballistic missile.
articles.body: Pakistan's Army has test-launched the Fatah-2 Extended Range hypersonic ballistic missile. The weapon carries advanced navigation and state-of-the-art avionics, and can engage targets with high precision and defeat enemy missile defences because of its trajectory and manoeuvrability, as per the Pakistani military. The launch was witnessed by the commander of the Army Rocket Force Command, senior officers, scientists and engineers. The extended range is expected to enhance Pakistan's reach and its ability to engage deep targets. The test also validated technical parameters of sub-systems meant to improve accuracy and survivability. No range figure was announced for the extended-range version.The Fatah-II is the successor to the Fatah-I and has a longer range and greater precision. In its standard form it is reported to have a range of about 400 km, uses inertial navigation combined with satellite guidance for mid-course correction, and has a terminal guidance system that adjusts its path in the final phase. It carries conventional warheads and is designed to strike military positions and radar installations. The test came days after Pakistan launched an extended-range version of the Fatah-4 ground-launched cruise missile.Fatah-II failed the Sindoor testThe tests come against the backdrop of Operation Sindoor. After the terror attack on civilians in Pahalgam, India struck nine terror targets deep inside Pakistani territory. Pakistan retaliated, and the tempo of operations peaked on May 10, when rocket attacks were intercepted by air defence missiles near the Sirsa air base. Within hours, Indian missile and drone strikes destroyed Pakistani air defence sites and BrahMos strikes hit key air bases, hampering flight operations until runways were repaired. This led to the Pakistani Directors General of Military Operation (DGMO) to call his counterpart to ask for a ceasefire. The failed missile strike, proving to IslamabadIndia is working on its own long-range strike options. The Army has inducted the Pinaka, Smerch, Pralay and BrahMos, and a Long Range Guided Rocket version of the Pinaka under development is meant to reach 120 km. The newest iteration of the BrahMos, which flies at near Mach 3, is expected to extend its range to as much as 800 km. The Army has traditionally relied on the Air Force for deep interdiction missions against command centres, ammunition dumps, bridges and logistics hubs, and missiles can now take on some of these targets.The case for this rests on air defence. India says an S-400 battery brought down a Pakistani aircraft from more than 300 km during Operation Sindoor, which shows how far modern air defences can reach. Against such networks, the use of non-stealth combat aircraft is limited, at a time when the Air Force is short of fighters. Using missiles against deep targets would free those fighters for other tasks.

articles.title: Jenny McCarthy co-hosted a pet competition that raised over $8 million to help complete a 25-acre wildlife rehabilitation centre in Washington
articles.summary: Every year, millions of pet owners treat their dogs and cats as family, and one national campaign turned that devotion into rescue funding.
articles.body: Every year, millions of pet owners treat their dogs and cats as family, and one national campaign turned that devotion into rescue funding. America's Favourite Pet, hosted by animal advocates Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg, invited the public to vote for animals online while raising money for a Washington-based nonprofit that rescues domestic animals and heals injured wildlife. The 2026 edition continued that mission, supporting an organisation whose newest facility is a twenty-five-acre wildlife rehabilitation centre. This article explains how the competition worked, where the donations went, what the funds ultimately built, and how ordinary pet owners took part nationwide.How the America's Favourite Pet 2026 online voting competition works for dog and cat owners nationwideAmerica's Favourite Pet is an annual online competition organised by Colossal, a professional fundraising organisation, according to the company's November 2025 news release. In 2026, dog and cat owners registered one companion per household by uploading a photo, then asked family, friends and social media followers to vote. Each voter received one free vote every twenty-four hours, and additional votes cost one dollar each, with that money directed to the beneficiary. Registration was open through January 12, 2026. The prize for winners was a $10,000 cash award and a cover feature in Modern Cat or Modern Dog magazine. Celebrity hosts Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg, both described by Colossal as devoted animal advocates, lent their voices to the campaign, although the Marblehead Current described the pair as its organisers.Where the money goes, rescuing domestic animals and rehabilitating injured wildlife in Washington StateMoney raised through the competition benefited the Progressive Animal Welfare Society (PAWS), a Washington-based nonprofit that rescues, rehabilitates and re-homes domestic animals and wildlife, according to Colossal. The Marblehead Current reported that the organisation rehabilitates orphaned and injured wildlife and shelters homeless cats and dogs. The nonprofit's chief executive officer, Heidi Wills, told supporters in the Colossal announcement that the campaign had helped the organisation rescue emaciated dogs from a hoarding situation, care for animals displaced by natural disasters, and meet urgent needs of countless cats, dogs and more than one hundred fifty species of wildlife. Colossal explained that it raised the funds through a public charity grantmaker that passed the money to the chosen beneficiary once each competition ended. That structure linked paid votes to rescue work.Inside the twenty-five-acre wildlife rehabilitation centre that campaign fundraising helped completeThe clearest tangible result of the fundraising was a twenty-five-acre wildlife rehabilitation centre in Washington State. Colossal's news release said the 2025 competition generated more than $8 million and that those funds supported the completion of the new facility. The same money, the release added, expanded educational programmes that reached more than 4,000 students nationwide. The centre sits within a broader mission; the Marblehead Current reported that the nonprofit rehabilitates orphaned and injured wildlife, while Wills told supporters the campaign's support reached more than one hundred fifty wildlife species. The 2026 competition carried that work forward. The official America's Favourite Pet website names two winners: Rockefeller, a nine-year-old Morkie from New York City who loves Central Park walks and games of fetch, and Sammy, a Ragdoll cat who enjoys sunbathing and turning everyday objects into miniature hockey games. The winning dog and cat appear on the covers of Modern Dog and Modern Cat magazines, where their owners share life with their companions. Neither report described the centre's layout, enclosures or animal capacity, so readers wanting those details should contact the organisation directly.More than twenty-two million dollars raised for animal rescue and wildlife careColossal said America's Favourite Pet had raised more than $22 million for the Washington-based nonprofit and was entering its sixth year when 2026 registration opened. In 2025 alone, the campaign generated more than $8 million, the news release stated, which funded care for thousands of domestic pets and injured wildlife. Wills credited the competition with allowing the organisation to answer urgent calls, from hoarding rescues to disaster response, as she told supporters in the announcement. Colossal also framed the project as a model for pet lovers and brands that wanted to combine passion with purpose, arguing that digital campaigns could deliver tangible results. The competition's official website shows the total has since grown: its beneficiary section says Colossal has raised over $29 million, while the homepage headline cites more than $7.5 million without explaining how that figure is measured. The 2026 edition, hosted by Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg, also recognised six runners-up: the dogs Betsy, Fendi Bell and James Dean and the cats Mr Midge, Asia and Jill. Sponsors Crown & Paw and Love, Nala supplied prizes, treats and surprises to competitors. Readers should note that Colossal is a professional fundraiser and that its figures came from its own announcement and website, so cautious donors may wish to review how the funds were granted.How local pet owners like Lolo the Labrador mix are rallying neighbours and supporters to vote and giveBehind the national numbers were local owners such as Leah Goodman of Marblehead, Massachusetts, whose lab mix Lolo reached the quarterfinals. "She just gives so much love," Goodman said when asked why her dog should win. Goodman also told the publication the contest was a fun project that gave back to a good cause. Lolo was born in Georgia, arrived at the Northeast Animal Shelter in Salem and was adopted at eight weeks old, according to the report. Quarterfinal voting stayed open until midnight Eastern time on February 27, and votes cast on February 18 counted twice. Future entrants can follow the same path, register a pet, share the voting link, and give a free daily vote or a one-dollar donation vote.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Thursday voiced concern and demanded a probe over an alleged plot to target a Hindu temple in the US,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Thursday voiced concern and demanded a probe over an alleged plot to target a Hindu temple in the US, saying the incident has heightened India’s concerns over the "growing racist hostility and anti-India hate" in the United States.Also Read | ‘Timely action’: India welcomes US response after Illinois teen held over Hindu temple attack plotThe MEA’s remarks came after US law enforcement agencies arrested a 19-year-old man, identified as Alexandros Paporakis, following an investigation into threats of a potential mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois.“We are deeply concerned by reports of an alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting targeting a Hindu temple in the Aurora region of Illinois. The reported anti-Hindu and racist nature of the alleged plot, including references to violence against people of Indian origin, is particularly disturbing,” the MEA said in a statement.“This incident adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US. There is a need for greater vigilance, zero tolerance for hate-motivated violence, and decisive action to ensure the safety and security of the Indian community,” it added.The MEA further stated that India expected US authorities to thoroughly investigate the matter, bring those responsible to justice and take the necessary steps to prevent similar incidents in the future.The alleged attack plotAccording to the Palatine Police Department, which probed the alleged plot and arrested Paporakis, the investigation began on October 11, when it received information from the Mount Prospect Police Department about a possible mass shooting. The tip came from an individual who reported receiving “concerning” electronic messages from Paporakis.Also Read | 'Where anti-Indian hatred can lead': US lawmaker Raja Krishnamoorthi's warning after plot targeting Aurora Hindu templeInvestigators found that Paporakis had shared a document outlining an alleged plan to carry out a mass shooting at the temple. He had also circulated images of a rifle, rifle magazines, body armour and other tactical equipment.Police arrested the suspect as he was leaving his home. A subsequent search of the residence yielded a rifle, several loaded rifle magazines, hundreds of additional rounds of ammunition, tactical equipment and other items linked to the investigation.Among the recovered items was a tactical vest fitted with body armour and a patch displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism.Detectives also examined electronic communications and a document attributed to Paporakis titled “Why I Fought: A.K.A.: (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto).” According to the police department, the document contained white supremacist and extremist views, including references to violence against people of South Asian heritage, particularly those of Indian descent.Investigators believe Paporakis may have been planning an attack on October 11, potentially targeting a Hindu place of worship in the Aurora area. Following the probe, police contacted Hindu places of worship within their jurisdiction to alert them to the reported threat.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: CJP's Dipke questions Imran Khan's 'Leave India' notice, cites Mary Millben's support for BJP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: CJP founder Abhijit Dipke on Thursday questioned the restrictions imposed on Bollywood actor Imran Khan after Mumbai Police issued him a ‘Leave
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CJP founder Abhijit Dipke on Thursday questioned the restrictions imposed on Bollywood actor Imran Khan after Mumbai Police issued him a ‘Leave India’ notice over his participation in protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Drawing a comparison with American singer Mary Millben, who has publicly expressed support for the BJP, Dipke questioned why Khan is facing immigration action.In a post on X, Dipke said, "Mary Millben, an American, can speak in favour of the BJP. But Imran, an OCI cardholder, can’t say anything against the BJP."The actor, 43, who is the nephew of Bollywood actor Aamir Khan, holds an American passport and an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, according to ANI. He has been directed to leave India by October 28 following his participation in the ongoing protests in Mumbai.Khan participated in a demonstration at August Kranti Maidan on October 10, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.A complaint was filed against Khan, following which the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) issued the notice directing him to leave the country for allegedly violating the Foreigners Act.According to ANI, action has been initiated under Sections 29 and 7 of the Immigration Act over allegations that he participated in a political protest despite not being an Indian citizen.ALSO READ: Imran Khan asked to leave India: What rights do OCI cardholders have?Khan was detained by Mumbai Police during the demonstration. After his detention, he posted a photograph on social media that appeared to show him inside a police van, with the caption: "Apparently I’m going for a drive."Speaking to the media, Khan said he had attended the protest without any specific demands."I don't have demands. I am here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I am here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted. Why are people's voices being suppressed? That is why I am here," he said.The notice followed demands by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya for Khan's arrest and deportation over his participation in the demonstration. Somaiya alleged that the actor had violated OCI provisions and visa conditions.Speaking to the media, Somaiya said, "The citizens of India cannot tolerate the political extremism that Imran Khan has been displaying during his recent stay in the country. He is an American citizen holding an OCI card, yet he has attempted to misuse his status."Earlier American singer Millben and Dipke exchanged barbs over allegations of foreign funding of the outfit. In a post on X, Millben claimed that the CJP is being "funded by donors" in the US and called upon all "young patriots" in India to rise and peacefully protest the "disruptive spirit" of the Dipke-founded outfit.Later Dipke questioned foreign interference in India’s internal affairs. Millben responded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had the support of “1.5 billion beautiful Indian citizens” and did not need American backing.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah likely to visit India in November-end; what's on agenda
articles.summary: Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah is expected to visit India in the third or fourth week of November, with both countries preparing for talks on major
articles.body: Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah is expected to visit India in the third or fourth week of November, with both countries preparing for talks on major infrastructure projects and longstanding disputes, including the boundary issue, air routes and trade.The three-day visit, which would be Shah’s first official bilateral trip abroad since taking office in March, is expected to focus on strengthening ties between Kathmandu and New Delhi. However, the dates have not been finalised, a high-level diplomatic source told the Kathmandu Post.Shah is expected to remain in New Delhi, where he will hold delegation-level talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and meet other senior ministers. The two sides are also expected to sign several agreements and memorandums of understanding.PM Modi had invited Balen Shah to visit India at a mutually convenient time soon after he was sworn in.Shah’s only overseas trip so far was to New York in September to attend the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal, who attended the same session, had said after returning to Nepal that the visit would take place at an appropriate time. He stressed that both governments wanted it to be “fruitful and result-oriented”.Infrastructure projects and new agreementsPreparations for the visit have already moved forward, with Nepal and India exchanging lists of projects that could be inaugurated during Shah’s trip, according to two senior Nepali foreign ministry officials.Projects being considered include the Nepal Police Academy in Panauti, Kavrepalanchok, a bridge in Darchula, the integrated check post in Bhairahawa and a motorable bridge over the Mahakali River.The two prime ministers are also expected to jointly mark the start of construction on the integrated check post at Dodhara Chandani, the Lower Arun hydropower project and a petroleum pipeline connecting Siliguri in India with Jhapa in Nepal.Major hydropower projects could feature prominently in the discussions, as most bilateral mechanisms have already held their meetings. These include the 750MW West Seti, the 480MW Phukot Karnali and the 450MW Seti River-6 projects, all of which involve India’s state-owned NHPC.Other proposals expected to be discussed include a project on the Koshi River, the Ayodhya-Janakpur railway link and Indian assistance for Nepal’s plans to develop its artificial intelligence sector.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘You lost a son, I lost my boyfriend’: Shraddha Dubey’s emotional message to Shiva Sharma’s mother
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: “It’s not like you have lost a son, I have lost my boyfriend,” said model and social media influencer Shraddha Dubey, the prime accused in the
articles.body: LUCKNOW: “It’s not like you have lost a son, I have lost my boyfriend,” said model and social media influencer Shraddha Dubey, the prime accused in the death of her live-in partner, 28-year-old restaurant owner Shiva Sharma, in a video released on Thursday.In a video, Dubey appealed to the media not to spread rumours about the incident, alleging that Sharma’s mother had accused her and others of murder without knowing the full circumstances. She also claimed that Sharma’s mother had quarrelled with her driver at the hospital.“Think why would someone kill someone and throw them from their own apartment,” she said, questioning the allegations against her.Dubey alleged that Sharma had been receiving calls from people he had borrowed money from and had repeatedly told her that he would die by suicide if he could not repay the loans.Recounting how they met, Dubey said she called Sharma twice, but he did not answer. He later called her at around 2am and asked to meet her. They went to Peddler’s Cafe, where he ordered coffee for her and juice for himself. She added that he had consumed “a lot of beers” before meeting her.“Later, both of us went to my place. While he drove my car, my driver took his car,” she said.Dubey said her sister, Rashmi, visited her home on October 8 to discuss a Navratri puja. She denied her sister’s involvement in the case, claiming that Rashmi barely knew Sharma. She said she and Rashmi went for a walk that evening, later joined by Sharma’s friends Ashwini Mishra and Harsh, before the group went on a long drive. Dubey also said she had spoken to Sharma’s mother, sister and brother-in-law that day.Recalling the events of October 9, when Sharma died, Dubey claimed that he appeared depressed. She said they woke up and made tea before he went to the washroom.“I don’t even know what it was. We woke up and made tea. Shiva went to the washroom. Usually, he would never close the main gate. But this time, he did. I asked my sister to check on him after a while. As soon as she opened the gate, he jumped from the balcony,” she said.Dubey also alleged that Sharma’s mother accused them of murder and assaulted her driver at the hospital.“It will be recorded on the hospital’s camera. Without knowing anything, she accused us of murder. Without thinking, she blamed us for murder. She blamed us so badly that we might not be able to get out of that blame for life,” she said.In an earlier video, Dubey denied any wrongdoing and claimed that Sharma had died by suicide. She also urged the media to stop linking her to politicians and senior officials, saying she was willing to appear before the police and record her statement.“I am not missing. I want to come before the police and tell them everything I know. I want to place the complete truth before them,” she said.She added that following someone on Instagram did not mean she knew them or had a relationship with them.Sharma died on October 9 after falling from the fourth floor of Awadh Green Apartment in Lucknow’s Hazratganj area. According to police sources, he had been in a relationship with Dubey for around four months.Following his death, Sharma’s mother, Ranjana Sharma, lodged an FIR accusing Dubey, her sister Rashmi, driver Adil and others of murder. The family has alleged that Dubey pushed Sharma from the building, a claim investigators are examining.Lucknow Police have announced a reward of Rs 25,000 each for information leading to the arrest of Dubey, her sister Rashmi Dubey and Tanveer Ali, alias Danish, in connection with the case.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: In 2006, an Oregon woman sold her $398,000 home to her son-in-law for $270,000 and says she was promised she could stay for life; 20 years later, an appeals court rejected that claimed life estate
articles.summary: An Oregon woman who sold her home to her son-in-law for $270,000 in 2006, despite the property being worth approximately $398,000, has lost a legal
articles.body: An Oregon woman who sold her home to her son-in-law for $270,000 in 2006, despite the property being worth approximately $398,000, has lost a legal dispute over her claimed right to live there for the rest of her life. The Oregon Court of Appeals ruled that the written sale documents transferred her entire ownership interest and did not reserve a life estate, a legal arrangement that would have allowed her to remain in the property for life.The dispute involved Kathleen Edwards and her son-in-law, Scott Short, who purchased the property with his brother. According to the court document, Edwards maintained that Short had promised she could continue living in the home until she died or decided to move out. However, Short denied granting her any permanent right to occupy the property, although he acknowledged allowing her to live there rent-free for some time.The disagreement reached court after Short asked Edwards to leave the property in January 2020, approximately 14 years after the sale. She refused, arguing that their original agreement allowed her to remain in the home for life. A trial court initially accepted her claim and ordered the property deed to be changed to recognise her life estate.However, the Oregon Court of Appeals overturned that decision. According to the court,the written documents clearly transferred all of Edwards' ownership rights and that evidence of an earlier oral promise could not be used to contradict those terms. The appellate court reversed the lower court's judgment and sent the case back for further proceedings.Financial difficulties led to the sale in 2006Edwards faced financial difficulties after her husband pleaded guilty to child sexual abuse in December 2005 and received a prison sentence. At the time, she had a mortgage of approximately $270,000 on her home and could no longer afford to continue living there.She considered several options, including taking out a reverse mortgage or renting rooms to tenants. Her daughter, who was married to Short, encouraged her husband to purchase the property.Short and his brother eventually agreed to buy the house for $270,000, the outstanding mortgage amount. The property's estimated market value at the time was approximately $398,000.Edwards claimed that when the purchase was discussed, Short promised they “would take care of everything,” including property taxes and homeowners' insurance. She also maintained that she had been assured she could remain in the house until her death or until she voluntarily moved elsewhere.However, Short disputed that account. While he acknowledged that Edwards had continued living in the house without paying rent but, he also said he had allowed it to avoid family conflict, not because she held a life estate.What the property documents saidThe parties signed three documents to complete the transaction including a warranty deed, a Land Sale Contract and a Memorandum of Contract of Sales.The warranty deed says that Edwards transferred “all of defendant’s right title and interest” in the property to Short and his brother. It contained no provision allowing Edwards to retain ownership rights or remain in the house for life.The Land Sale Contract also stated that it represented the “entire, final and complete agreement” between the parties and replaced their earlier written or oral agreements concerning the property.After the documents were signed and the deed recorded, Short began paying the mortgage, property taxes and insurance. Within a year, his brother transferred his ownership interest to Short, leaving him as the sole owner.Court initially ruled in Edwards' favourAfter Edwards refused to leave in 2020, Short filed a lawsuit seeking possession of the property and confirmation of his ownership rights.Edwards argued that the written documents did not reflect the full agreement. She said the promise that she could “live there until I die” had created a life estate.Following a three-day trial, the lower court accepted her position. It found that the documents did not fully record the parties' understanding and allowed evidence of their earlier conversations.The court concluded that Edwards had established the alleged life estate agreement by clear and convincing evidence. It also found that a purported lease, although ineffective, had been an attempt to record her right to remain in the property.The trial court consequently ordered the warranty deed to be amended to recognise her life estate. Short appealed the decision.Why appeals court overturned rulingThe Court of Appeals examined whether evidence of the alleged oral promise could legally be considered when the written documents contained different terms.Its decision centred on the parol evidence rule, which generally prevents earlier oral agreements from being used to contradict the terms of a final written contract.The judges found that the transaction documents represented the parties' complete agreement. They also noted that a life estate was a significant property interest that would not ordinarily be omitted from a deed.Because the warranty deed transferred Edwards' entire ownership interest without any stated exception, the court concluded that the alleged oral agreement directly conflicted with its terms.The appeals court therefore ruled that the trial court had wrongly admitted evidence of the earlier promise and wrongly amended the deed.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2023, South Andaman’s Rajeshwari had just five backyard birds and no scientific poultry experience; today her expanded unit produces about 2,000 chicks a month and an estimated ₹1.91 lakh monthly net profit
articles.summary: In 2023, Rajeshwari, a 38-year-old woman from Wandoor village in South Andaman, had just five indigenous birds in her backyard.
articles.body: In 2023, Rajeshwari, a 38-year-old woman from Wandoor village in South Andaman, had just five indigenous birds in her backyard. She had no experience in scientific poultry management and kept the birds mainly for household consumption. Today, she runs an organised poultry enterprise that produces around 2,000 chicks every month and generates an estimated monthly net profit of ₹1.91 lakh. According to the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), Rajeshwari's growth from a small backyard poultry keeper to a rural entrepreneur followed training, technical guidance and the adoption of scientific poultry farming practices. Her enterprise now supplies poultry meat, chicks and table eggs, creating a regular source of income.From five backyard birds to a poultry enterpriseRajeshwari holds an M.Sc. degree in Botany. In 2023, looking for a sustainable source of self-employment, she approached the ICAR-Central Island Agricultural Research Institute (ICAR-CIARI) in Sri Vijaya Puram for guidance on poultry farming. According to the official website of ICAR, she initially had only five indigenous birds and no prior experience in scientific poultry management. The institute enrolled her in a skill development programme that included practical training and continued technical support. She learnt about poultry housing, flock management, healthcare, vaccination, feed formulation and enterprise planning. As she gained experience, she gradually expanded her backyard unit and began treating poultry farming as a business rather than an activity meant mainly for household use.ICAR-CIARI continued to monitor her progress and provide guidance. She later received advanced training in brooder, grower and breeder management, hatchery operations, disease prevention and the scheduling of production activities. These practices helped her organise poultry rearing and chick production to support a more regular flow of income throughout the year.How she produces around 2,000 chicks every monthWith technical support from ICAR-CIARI, Rajeshwari established a semi-intensive poultry unit with a mini-incubator that has a setter capacity of 2,500 eggs. According to ICAR, she initially reared 2,400 birds using scientific management practices. She gradually developed a breeder flock that could support continuous chick production. From the fifth month onwards, she maintained around 550 birds as parental stock for chick production. At the same time, she reared nearly 1,200 birds for meat production and sale.Her breeder flock now produces approximately 3,600 eggs a month. Of these, around 2,500 are used for hatching. With improved incubation techniques and scientific health management, she achieves a hatchability rate of nearly 80%, producing about 2,000 chicks every month. This production system allows her to manage different parts of the poultry business together, from maintaining breeding birds to producing chicks and raising birds for meat.₹1.91 lakh estimated monthly net profitThe financial figures reported by ICAR-CIARI show the scale of Rajeshwari's enterprise. According to the ICAR’s website, she currently markets approximately 600 kg of live poultry meat, 600 chicks and 1,100 table eggs every month. The integrated poultry unit generates an estimated monthly net profit of around ₹1.91 lakh. That makes it a benefit-cost ratio of 2.02 for the enterprise, indicating that the activity has been financially viable under the conditions in the Andaman Islands. These figures reflect the combined output of her poultry operation rather than income from chick sales alone. The business includes meat birds, chicks and table eggs, giving her multiple products to sell.Scientific training helped her expandRajeshwari's experience highlights the role of technical training in helping small-scale poultry keepers move towards organised production. Instead of relying only on traditional backyard rearing, she learnt how to manage poultry health, feeding, breeding and incubation as connected parts of a business. According to ICAR-CIARI, her progress has also encouraged rural youth and women in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to consider scientific poultry farming as a possible source of self-employment. Her journey began with five birds kept mainly for household consumption. With training, continued guidance and a gradual expansion of operations, she has built a unit that produces thousands of chicks and supplies poultry products every month.You use AI every day. articles.title: What is causing the haze in Southeast Asia? Key facts explained
articles.summary: Prolonged wildfires across Indonesia have led to a sharp rise in respiratory illnesses and spread dangerous haze across several Southeast asian nations.
articles.body: Prolonged wildfires across Indonesia have led to a sharp rise in respiratory illnesses and spread dangerous haze across several Southeast asian nations. Singapore and Malaysia have been among the worst affected over the past week.The worsening pollution has also heightened regional tensions, with officials raising concerns over Jakarta’s response to the fires and its reluctance to accept assistance from neighbouring countries.What is causing the haze?The haze is primarily caused by smoke and emissions from forest and peatland fires in Indonesia, particularly across Borneo and Sumatra. These islands have extensive forest cover and large peatland areas that become highly susceptible to fires during the dry season, which generally lasts from April to October.The region is also experiencing the effects of severe “super El Niño” conditions, which have intensified heat and dryness, allowing fires to spread more rapidly.Indonesia last witnessed fires of a comparable intensity in 2015, when similarly severe El Niño conditions contributed to widespread burning.How extensive is the damage caused by the fires?Official figures on the area affected by the fires have not been updated since July, when approximately 202,000 hectares, or around 500,000 acres, had reportedly burned.However, environmental organisation Auriga estimated that more than 637,000 hectares had been affected between January and August this year. The area is roughly nine times the size of Singapore.Deforestation monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has reported an even higher estimate, placing the affected area at nearly 900,000 hectares.How severe is the haze?Data from fire emissions watch, a platform developed by the European union’s copernicus climate monitoring service, showed that Indonesia had recorded the world’s highest fire emissions for a month. The country accounted for nearly half of global fire emissions during the preceding seven days.Indonesia’s air pollution index recorded readings exceeding 1,000 in some parts of Borneo and Sumatra. Pollution levels of 300 or above are already classified as hazardous.Singapore also experienced a significant deterioration in air quality. On Wednesday, the one-hour PM2.5 concentration in the western part of the island reached 284 micrograms per cubic metre, entering the national environment agency’s “very high” category for the first time this year.The health impact has been substantial. Indonesian Health Ministry data showed that respiratory illness cases associated with the fires had climbed to 283,270 across seven provinces as of October 13. This was more than twice the 113,336 cases recorded on September 9.The haze has also disrupted daily life and transport. Numerous schools in Indonesia, neighbouring East Timor and several Malaysian states have been forced to close. In Indonesia, nearly 2,000 flights were affected between August 11 and October 12.What measures is Indonesia taking to contain the fires?The Indonesian government has maintained that it is taking extensive measures to control the fires.More than 60,000 personnel have been deployed for firefighting operations, while around 50 aircraft have been involved in water-bombing and cloud-seeding efforts.Jakarta also plans to recruit additional forest rangers to strengthen fire prevention and has pledged to rehabilitate peatland ecosystems. Peatland fires are particularly difficult to extinguish because they can continue smouldering underground for extended periods, even at relatively low temperatures.The government has also said it is taking action against businesses and individuals violating regulations, including restrictions on using fire to clear agricultural land.Police officials have indicated that 223 individuals and nine companies could face action over their alleged involvement in starting forest fires.Why is Indonesia facing criticism?Indonesia has faced mounting international pressure to strengthen its efforts to prevent fires and respond more effectively once they break out.Despite government restrictions, the practice of burning land to clear it for cultivation has continued. Rapid deforestation to expand agricultural production, particularly palm oil cultivation, has also increased fire risks. The loss of forest cover and the draining of underground water sources can leave the soil drier and more vulnerable to burning.Jakarta has also faced questions over its decision not to declare the situation a national disaster. Such a declaration could enable the government to mobilise resources more quickly.Its reluctance to accept assistance offered by Malaysia and Singapore has further fuelled criticism, as the haze continues to affect countries across the region.How long could the fires and haze continue?Indonesian authorities have warned that the situation is unlikely to be brought under control until the region receives sustained rainfall.The dry season began earlier than usual this year and has continued for longer than expected. Although rainfall typically starts in October, forecasts suggest the onset of the rainy season could be delayed until November.Indonesia’s weather agency has said the effects of El Niño could persist until the first quarter of 2027. However, the arrival of seasonal rains is expected to help reduce the intensity of the fires and limit their wider impact.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1926, Tampa Theatre opened beneath a twinkling indoor night sky; 100 years later, it reopened after a seven-month, $24.5 million restoration of its historic auditorium
articles.summary: In 1926, visitors to Tampa Theatre in Florida could watch a film beneath a ceiling designed to resemble a night sky, complete with twinkling stars and
articles.body: In 1926, visitors to Tampa Theatre in Florida could watch a film beneath a ceiling designed to resemble a night sky, complete with twinkling stars and drifting clouds. A century later, the historic movie palace has reopened after a seven-month, $24.5 million restoration that refreshed its famous auditorium while upgrading the building for future audiences. The theatre officially opened on October 15, 1926. Its restored Duncan Auditorium welcomed visitors back in October 2026, ahead of its centennial celebration on the exact anniversary of its opening.As reported by American media portal Tampa Bay 28, the restoration involved everything from decorative paint and plaster to plumbing, electrical systems, sound and lighting. The work was part of the first phase of the theatre's Second Century Campaign, which aims to preserve the historic venue and expand its cultural and educational activities.A century-old night sky gets a new lookOne of Tampa Theatre's most recognisable features is its Ruberg Night Sky, an atmospheric ceiling that gives the auditorium the appearance of an open-air courtyard at night. The restoration upgraded the lighting so the ceiling's stars could twinkle with new technology. New LED lighting also allows the auditorium to create sunrise and sunset effects. The project included work on the ceiling's cloud effects, too. As reported by Creative Loafing Tamp, the theatre originally opened with a machine that projected wispy clouds across the ceiling. The original 1926 machine was not available for use, so the technical team restored an older machine believed to date from the 1950s or 1960s.Restoring the auditorium to its 1926 appearanceThe restoration was not limited to adding new technology. Workers also studied the building's original finishes to bring back its early appearance. As reported by WUSF, restoration specialists carried out forensic paint analysis to identify the original colours beneath later layers. Some areas that appeared to be one colour had different shades underneath. Tampa Theatre CEO George Leveque told WUSF that the aim was for the auditorium to look as it did when it opened in 1926. The restoration was led by EverGreene Architectural Arts, a firm specialising in historic buildings.The project also addressed the less visible parts of the century-old structure. According to Tampa Bay 28, the work included replacing old plumbing, installing new electrical systems and upgrading sound and lighting equipment. Leveque described the project as a restoration of both the visible historic features and the systems that keep the building functioning.Forgotten objects emerged during constructionThe work also brought old pieces of Tampa Theatre's history back into view. As staff cleared storage areas to make room for new educational facilities, they found furniture, lamps, tables and paintings that had been kept inside the building for years. Some of the objects dated back to the theatre's early days. According to Tampa Bay 28, staff used photographs from 1926 to work out where some of the paintings had originally hung, with plans to return them to their former places.The theatre also worked with the University of South Florida to digitally scan objects that could not be physically restored. The scans created digital records of historic items that might otherwise have been lost. Creative Loafing Tampa separately reported that a burgundy tapestry from the theatre's 1926 opening was among the historic items restored and returned to its original place.A new education centre for the next generationThe $24.5 million first phase of the Second Century Campaign also includes a dedicated education wing. The theatre plans to use the new space for film camps, classes, birthday parties and other community programmes. According to the official website of Tampa theatre, the project repurposes underused space to create more than 3,000 square feet for educational activities. Until now, many educational programmes had to share the main auditorium with film screenings and other events. The new classrooms will allow the theatre to run more activities without competing for the same space. The project also includes accessibility improvements and updated technology for films, live performances and other events. New infrastructure, including heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems, is intended to improve comfort and reduce operating costs.Community support helped fund the restorationThe restoration was supported by donors and public funding. Tampa Theatre's campaign page describes the Second Century Campaign as an effort to preserve the building while expanding its role as a cultural and community venue. Tampa Bay 28 reported that one donor who had not previously contributed made the largest single gift in the theatre's history to support restoration of the night sky. Six weeks later, another donor made a major gift for the education centre.A new chapter after 100 yearsTampa Theatre's centennial falls on October 15, 2026, exactly 100 years after it first opened. The anniversary celebration includes a programme featuring the silent comedy Sherlock Jr., accompanied by the Paragon Ragtime Orchestra and the theatre's Mighty Wurlitzer Theatre Organ, according to the official event page of the theatre.You use AI every day.
